lessons.title: Lists
lessons.summary: Ordered collections: indexing, changing, adding, removing, sorting and looping.

sections.heading: Many values under one name
sections.body:
A **list** holds any number of values, in order, inside square brackets: `toppings = ["cheese", "ham", "olives"]`. Lists can hold any type, mixed, and even other lists. `[]` is an empty list.

Lists use the same **indexing** and **slicing** as strings: `toppings[0]` is the first item, `toppings[-1]` the last, `toppings[1:]` everything but the first. `len(toppings)` is how many items there are, and `"ham" in toppings` checks membership.

sections.heading: Lists can change
sections.body: Unlike strings, lists are **mutable**: you can change them in place. Assign to an index to replace an item. These methods change the list itself:

example.code:
orders = ["margherita", "pepperoni"]
orders.append("veggie")
orders[0] = "hawaiian"
first = orders.pop(0)
print(first, orders, len(orders))

bullets: `.append(x)`: add x to the end. The most-used one by far.
`.insert(i, x)`: add x at position i.
`.remove(x)`: remove the first x (ValueError if it's not there).
`.pop()`: remove and return the last item; `.pop(i)` the one at i.
`.sort()`: sort in place. `sorted(lst)` returns a new sorted list instead, leaving the original alone.

sections.heading: Looping and building
sections.body:
`for item in some_list:` goes through each item. To build a new list, start with `[]` and `.append` in a loop. Built-in functions `sum`, `min`, `max` and `len` work directly on lists of numbers.

Careful: the methods that change a list return `None`. `orders = orders.sort()` sorts it and then throws it away, leaving `orders` as None. Either call `orders.sort()` on its own line, or use `orders = sorted(orders)`.

sections.heading: Two names, one list
sections.body: Assigning a list to another name doesn't copy it: `b = a` makes both names refer to the **same** list, so changing it through one name shows through the other. Use `b = a.copy()` or `b = a[:]` when you want a separate copy. This is the cause of many confusing bugs, so it's worth remembering.

key_points: `[a, b, c]` is a list; index and slice like strings.
Lists are mutable: `.append`, `.insert`, `.remove`, `.pop`, assigning to an index.
`.sort()` changes the list and returns None; `sorted()` returns a new one.
`b = a` shares the list; `a.copy()` makes a separate one.
mistakes: Writing `items = items.append(x)`, which sets items to None.
Indexing past the end, which is an IndexError.
Changing a list through one name and being surprised it changed through another.
lessons.try_it: Make a list of five numbers. Append one, remove one, sort it, and print the smallest, largest and total. Make `b = a`, append to b, and print a to see the sharing for yourself.

quiz.question: What's `["a", "b", "c"][-2]`?
quiz.explain: -1 is the last item and -2 the one before it.

quiz.question: After `x = [3, 1, 2]` and `x = x.sort()`, what's x?
quiz.explain: sort changes the list and returns None, which then gets assigned to x.

quiz.question: `a = [1]`, `b = a`, `b.append(2)`. What's a?
quiz.explain: a and b are the same list, so appending through b changes it for a too.

lessons.title: Dictionaries
lessons.summary: Looking things up by key: adding, reading safely, looping and counting.

sections.heading: Values stored by name
sections.body: A **dictionary** (dict) stores **key-value pairs**: you look a value up by its key instead of by position. It's written with curly brackets, a colon between each key and value, and commas between pairs. Keys are usually strings or numbers and must be unique.

example.code:
menu = {"margherita": 8.5, "pepperoni": 9.75, "veggie": 9.0}
print(menu["pepperoni"])
menu["hawaiian"] = 10.25
menu["veggie"] = 8.75
print(len(menu), "pizzas on the menu")
example.explain: Assigning to a new key adds it; assigning to an existing key replaces its value.

sections.heading: Reading safely
sections.body:
Reading a key that isn't there, like `menu["calzone"]`, raises a `KeyError`. Two ways to avoid it: check first with `if "calzone" in menu:` (which checks keys), or use `.get`: `menu.get("calzone")` gives `None` if it's missing, and `menu.get("calzone", 0)` gives the default you choose.

`del menu["veggie"]` removes a pair, and `.pop(key)` removes it and returns its value.

sections.heading: Looping over a dictionary
sections.body: `for key in menu:` loops over the keys. `.values()` gives just the values, and `.items()` gives key and value together, which you unpack in the loop: `for name, price in menu.items():`. Dictionaries remember the order keys were added in.

sections.heading: The counting pattern
sections.body: One of the most useful patterns in programming: counting how many times each thing appears. Loop through the things, and for each one, add 1 to its count in a dictionary, starting from 0 if it isn't there yet. `.get(key, 0) + 1` does exactly that.

example.code:
orders = ["veggie", "pepperoni", "veggie", "margherita", "veggie"]
counts = {}
for pizza in orders:
    counts[pizza] = counts.get(pizza, 0) + 1
print(counts)
best = max(counts, key=counts.get)
print(best)
example.explain: Prints `{'veggie': 3, 'pepperoni': 1, 'margherita': 1}` then `veggie`. `max` with `key=counts.get` picks the key with the biggest count.

key_points: `{key: value}` maps keys to values; `d[key]` reads, `d[key] = v` sets.
Missing keys raise KeyError. Use `in` or `.get(key, default)`.
`.items()` loops over keys and values together.
mistakes: Reading a missing key with square brackets.
Expecting `x in d` to search the values. It checks keys.
Changing a dictionary's size while looping over it.
lessons.try_it: Make a dictionary of three friends' names and ages. Add a fourth, change one age, and print each name and age with `.items()`. Count the letters in your name with the counting pattern.

quiz.question: What does `{"a": 1}.get("b", 0)` give?
quiz.explain: b isn't a key, so get returns the default you gave, 0.

quiz.question: With `d = {"x": 5}`, what's `5 in d`?
quiz.explain: in checks the keys, not the values. Use `5 in d.values()` for values.

quiz.question: What does `d["k"] = d.get("k", 0) + 1` do the first time, when k isn't in d?
quiz.explain: get gives 0 because k is missing, plus 1 makes 1.

lessons.title: Tuples, sets and comprehensions
lessons.summary: Fixed pairs, collections without duplicates, and building lists in one line.

sections.heading: Tuples
sections.body:
A **tuple** is like a list that can't be changed: `point = (3, 4)`. Use tuples for small fixed groups of values that belong together, like coordinates, or a name and a score. You've already used them: `return a, b` returns a tuple, and `for name, price in menu.items()` unpacks one each iteration.

Because they can't change, tuples can be dictionary keys and set items, which lists can't.

sections.heading: Sets
sections.body:
A **set** holds unique values with no order: `{"cheese", "ham"}`, or `set()` for an empty one (`{}` is an empty dict). Adding something that's already there does nothing, so `set(a_list)` removes duplicates.

Checking `x in a_set` is very fast, even for huge sets. Sets also do maths: `a | b` (everything in either), `a & b` (only in both) and `a - b` (in a but not b).

example.explain: Prints `{'cheese'}`, then all four toppings in order, then `2`.

sections.heading: Comprehensions
sections.body:
A **list comprehension** builds a new list from another sequence in one line: `[expression for item in sequence]`, optionally with `if condition` at the end to keep only some items. It does the same job as an empty list plus a for loop with append, more compactly.

There are dict and set versions too: `{key: value for ...}` and `{value for ...}`. Keep them simple; if a comprehension needs nested loops and several conditions, a normal loop is clearer.

example.code:
prices = [8.5, 12.0, 9.25, 15.0]
with_tax = [round(p * 1.2, 2) for p in prices]
cheap = [p for p in prices if p < 10]
lengths = {word: len(word) for word in ["ham", "olives"]}
print(with_tax, cheap, lengths)

key_points: Tuples `(a, b)` are fixed groups; they unpack into names.
Sets hold unique values; `set(list)` removes duplicates; `&`, `|`, `-` compare sets.
`[expr for x in seq if cond]` builds a list in one line.
Use a normal loop when a comprehension gets complicated.
mistakes: Writing `{}` for an empty set (it's a dict; use `set()`).
Trying to change a tuple, which is a TypeError.
Comprehensions so long they need scrolling.
lessons.try_it: Turn a list with duplicates into a sorted list of unique values. Use a comprehension to make a list of the squares of 1 to 10, then only the even squares.

quiz.question: What's `len({1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3})`?
quiz.explain: A set keeps each value once: 1, 2 and 3.

quiz.question: What does `{}` create?
quiz.explain: Empty curly brackets make a dict. An empty set is `set()`.
